ImageDescription.value:
cross section: Young stem: Helianthus magnification: 400x

All vascular tissues in Helianthus are the product of primary growth. There are no signs of secondary growth (growth rings or lateral meristems) as might be seen in woody stems. 

Stomata may be seen in the single layered epidermis. Large multicellular trichomes are present and abundant in older stems.

The cortex consists of an outermost hypodermis of collenchyma, a deeper layer of parenchyma and a deepest band of endodermis (starch sheath).

The stele is defined by a ring of vascular bundles separated from one another by medullary rays of parenchyma cells.

Each vascular bundle consists of an outer supportive cap of sclerenchyma fibers (phloem fiber cap), a deeper layer of primary phloem with well defined sieve tubes and companion cells, and a deepest layer of primary xylem. In between the xylem and phloem, a narrow band of cambium my be seen.

In some preparations the highly lignified cells walls of xylem and sclerenchyma are stained red orange. These cells are dead at maturity and can also be distinguished by a heavy cell wall and absence of cytoplasmic contents.

The center of the stem is occupied by a pith of parenchyma cells that contain numerous starch storing amyloplasts.
